14:T9114,<p>You call <code>setState</code>, and the screen does not change on that line. What you've done is schedule a rerender. React runs it, writes the result into the DOM, and the browser still has to turn that DOM into pixels before anything changes on screen.</p>
<p>Take a search box. You type "a". The input should show "a", and the result list below it should filter down. Between your keystroke and those pixels there are nine steps. React owns the first three and the last; the browser owns the five in the middle, the same work it does with or without a framework.</p>
<pre><code>setState
  → render           ┐
  → commit           │  React
  → useLayoutEffect  ┘
  → Style Recalc     ┐
  → Render Tree      │
  → Layout           │  browser
  → Paint            │
  → Composite        ┘
  → useEffect           React (usually here; section IX has the exceptions)
</code></pre>
<h2>I. The render phase</h2>
<p>React calls your component function again. The function returns a new tree of plain JavaScript objects, often called the Virtual DOM. The browser has no idea this tree exists. It's just memory.</p>
<p>React compares the new tree against the previous one. Two rules govern the diff:</p>
<ul>
<li>Different element type at the same spot (a <code>&#x3C;div></code> became a <code>&#x3C;section></code>)? Tear down the old subtree, build a new one.</li>
<li>List items? The <code>key</code> prop tells React which item is which across renders.</li>
</ul>
<p>Since React 18, this phase can be paused and restarted. With <code>startTransition</code>, you mark an update as low priority. According to <a href="https://react.dev/reference/react/useTransition">react.dev</a>, if a more urgent update arrives before that render finishes, React drops the partial render, handles the urgent update, and then starts the low-priority render again. Nothing has touched the DOM yet, so throwing away the unfinished work is safe.</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="jsx" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="jsx" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">const</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> [</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">input</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">, </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">setInput</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">] </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1"> useState</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">(</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62">''</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">)</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">const</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> [</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">query</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">, </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">setQuery</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">] </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1"> useState</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">(</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62">''</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">)</span></span>

<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">function</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1"> handleChange</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">(</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#FFAB70;--shiki-light:#E36209">e</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">) {</span></span>

React can interrupt this render</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">  })</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">}</span></span>
<span data-line=""> </span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// &#x3C;ExpensiveList> rerenders with query.</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// If the user types again before it finishes, React drops</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// the ongoing render and restarts with the latest query.</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>Without <code>startTransition</code>, an update from a keystroke renders synchronously in one go. The input lags until the list finishes.</p>
<h2>II. The commit phase</h2>
<p>The diff is ready: in the search box, the input's value changes to "a", and a dozen list items get removed. React writes those changes to the real DOM.</p>
<p>This phase cannot be interrupted. Once the DOM starts changing, stopping halfway would leave a half-updated page on screen, so React runs it to completion.</p>
<p>Internally, in <a href="https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberCommitWork.js"><code>ReactFiberCommitWork.js</code></a>, commit runs three stages:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Before mutation</strong>: read what the DOM looks like before it changes. Class components use <code>getSnapshotBeforeUpdate</code> here to record things like scroll position.</li>
<li><strong>Mutation</strong>: actual DOM writes. <code>insertBefore</code>, <code>removeChild</code>, <code>setAttribute</code>. Old refs are detached and the previous <code>useLayoutEffect</code> cleanups run here.</li>
<li><strong>Layout</strong>: attach the new refs, fire <code>useLayoutEffect</code>. So "useLayoutEffect runs after commit" really means it runs inside the last of these three.</li>
</ul>
<p><span id="uselayouteffect"></span></p>
<h2>III. useLayoutEffect</h2>
<p>Before the browser paints anything, React fires <code>useLayoutEffect</code> synchronously.</p>
<p>A tooltip shows why this matters. It should sit below its button, unless there's no room below, in which case it flips above. You can't know that until the tooltip is in the DOM and you measure its height. <code>useLayoutEffect</code> is the last moment to measure (<code>getBoundingClientRect</code>, <code>offsetHeight</code>, scroll position) and fix the DOM before the user sees anything. As <a href="https://react.dev/reference/react/useLayoutEffect">react.dev</a> points out, if you measure in <code>useEffect</code> instead and then set state to move the tooltip, the browser may already have painted it in the wrong place, and the user sees it jump.</p>
<p>A tooltip opened by a click jumps too. Tested on headless Chrome 156: click a button, the tooltip renders below it, <code>useEffect</code> measures its height and calls <code>setState</code> to flip it above. In both React 18.3.1 and 19.3.1, 10 of 10 runs painted a frame with the tooltip below before it moved. With <code>useLayoutEffect</code>, all 10 painted it above from the first frame.</p>
<p>After a click, <code>useEffect</code> itself does run before the paint (section IX measures it). So why the jump? The effect running early doesn't mean the render its <code>setState</code> starts also finishes before the paint. React gives updates a priority, and a click's update is the highest, so React renders it right away. In the source of both 18.3.1 and 19.3.1, an update scheduled inside an effect after a click gets <code>DefaultEventPriority</code>, lower than the click. React doesn't render a default-priority update right away; it hands it to its Scheduler, which runs it in a separate task. React doesn't promise that task comes before the browser's next paint, and in all 10 runs the paint came first.</p>
<p>Reading layout is <strong>synchronous and blocking</strong>, for every entry on the <a href="https://gist.github.com/paulirish/5d52fb081b3570c81e3a">list of properties that force layout</a>: <code>getBoundingClientRect()</code> computes style and layout on that line, no Promise, no <code>await</code> to warn you. A read forces that compute only when layout is <em>dirty</em>, and a <strong>write</strong> dirties it. One read is one pass:</p>
<pre><code>read → style recalc → layout
</code></pre>
<p>Interleave writes and each one re-dirties, so the pass runs again and again (<strong>layout thrashing</strong>):</p>
<pre><code>read → style recalc → layout → write → style recalc → layout → write → style recalc → layout
</code></pre>
<p>Fix: batch all reads, then all writes. For pure measurement, <code>ResizeObserver</code> / <code>IntersectionObserver</code> report asynchronously, no forced layout.</p>
<p>Commit just wrote to the DOM, so layout is dirty when <code>useLayoutEffect</code> starts. The first read inside it runs Style Recalc, Render Tree and Layout right there, before the call returns. In that case sections IV to VI happen early, inside the effect, and the browser reuses the result unless the effect writes again. A trace recorded on headless Chrome 156, writing to the DOM and then calling <code>getBoundingClientRect()</code> once, shows 16 nested events between the call and its return, the same 16 in each of three runs. Among them, in order, are <code>Document::recalcStyle</code>, <code>Document::rebuildLayoutTree</code> and <code>Layout</code>, one for each of those sections; the rest are wrappers such as <code>Document::UpdateStyleAndLayout</code> and finer steps inside them.</p>
<p><code>useLayoutEffect</code> blocks the paint. Keep it fast.</p>
<p>Now the browser takes over.</p>
<blockquote>
<p><strong>CRP, technically.</strong> People call this whole pipeline (Style Recalc through Composite) the Critical Rendering Path. Strictly, by <a href="https://web.dev/learn/performance/understanding-the-critical-path">web.dev</a>'s definition, CRP is the path to the <em>first</em> render of a page. After that, <code>setState</code> reuses the same steps, but it isn't CRP anymore: CRP is about which resources (HTML, CSS, parser-blocking scripts) the first render has to wait for.</p>
</blockquote>
<p><span id="style-recalc"></span></p>
<h2>IV. Style Recalc</h2>
<p>The DOM changed, so the browser has to work out what every affected element should look like. In the terms of <a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/css-cascade-5/#value-stages">CSS Cascade 5 §4</a>, one property value on one element moves through six stages before it reaches the screen:</p>
<pre><code>declared → cascaded → specified → computed → used → actual
</code></pre>
<p>Style Recalc runs the first four (the steps below). <em>Used</em> and <em>actual</em> finish later, in Layout and Paint.</p>
<p><strong>Collecting.</strong> The browser gathers styles from three sources: its own builtin defaults (User Agent), any preferences the user has configured in their browser, and your stylesheet (Author).</p>
<p><strong>Cascading.</strong> All collected declarations compete. The browser resolves conflicts in the order <a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/css-cascade-5/#cascade-sort">CSS Cascade 5 §6.1</a> gives, highest priority first:</p>
<ol>
<li>Transitions</li>
<li>User Agent + <code>!important</code></li>
<li>User + <code>!important</code></li>
<li>Author + <code>!important</code></li>
<li>Animations</li>
<li>Author</li>
<li>User</li>
<li>User Agent</li>
</ol>
<p>Within the same origin and importance, the <code>style</code> attribute beats any stylesheet rule. Next come cascade layers (<code>@layer</code>); after that, specificity: IDs beat classes, classes beat type selectors. If specificity is equal, the declaration that appears last wins. The reference below gives example selectors and their scores. It puts the <code>style</code> attribute and <code>!important</code> on the same scale, as 1-0-0-0 and 1-0-0-0-0; that is a memory aid, since in the spec neither is part of specificity.</p>
<iframe src="https://specificity.webcore.io/" width="100%" height="800" style="border:none; margin: 24px 0;" title="CSS Specificity Reference"></iframe>
<p><strong>Defaulting.</strong> Properties with no declared value still need one. Two ways to fill it:<br>
Text-ish properties inherit from the parent: <code>color</code>, <code>font-size</code>, <code>font-family</code>.<br>
Box-ish properties fall back to a spec default: <code>border-style</code> → <code>none</code>, <code>margin</code> → <code>0</code>.<br>
Override either path with <code>inherit</code>, <code>initial</code>, <code>unset</code>, or <code>revert</code>.</p>
<p><strong>Resolving (the easy half).</strong> First of two passes (<a href="#layout-reflow">section VI</a> is the other). Anything that doesn't need geometry becomes concrete. <code>em</code> resolves against the element's own font size (<code>padding: 1em</code> on a 20px element is 20px); only inside <code>font-size</code> itself does it use the parent's. <code>rem</code> resolves against the root, <code>bold</code> becomes <code>700</code>, relative paths become absolute URLs. Anything that needs the box size (<code>50%</code>, <code>auto</code>, <code>min-content</code>) can't resolve yet, so it waits for Layout.</p>
<p>Output: every node's <em>computed style</em>. Note <em>computed</em>: <code>width: 50%</code> is still <code>50%</code> here, not a pixel. You can see this from JavaScript: on an element with <code>display: none</code> (no box, no layout), <code>getComputedStyle(el).width</code> returns <code>50%</code>. Show the element and the same call returns <code>400px</code>, because for laid-out elements it reports the value after Layout.</p>
<h2>V. Render Tree</h2>
<p>DOM plus computed styles merge into the Render Tree (Chrome calls it the layout tree). It's the DOM with style attached, minus the nodes that take up no space, plus a few that aren't in the DOM at all.</p>
<p><code>display: none</code>: excluded. No node in the tree, no space in the layout.<br>
<code>visibility: hidden</code>: included. Space reserved, pixels not drawn.<br>
<code>&#x3C;title></code>, <code>&#x3C;head></code>, <code>&#x3C;script></code>: excluded, because the browser's default stylesheet gives them <code>display: none</code>.<br>
<code>::before</code> / <code>::after</code> with <code>content</code>: included. <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/inside-browser-part3">Inside look, part 3</a> notes they go into the layout tree even though they're not DOM nodes.</p>
<p><span id="layout-reflow"></span></p>
<h2>VI. Layout / Reflow</h2>
<p>The browser walks the Render Tree and calculates the geometry of every element: position, width, height. This step is also called Reflow. In the search box, the list just lost a dozen items, so its height shrinks and everything below it moves up. Two CSS steps finish here:</p>
<p><strong>Formatting.</strong> The browser organizes elements into formatting contexts: block, inline, flex, grid. Each context has rules for how its children stack and flow.</p>
<p><strong>Resolving (the layout half).</strong> The second pass. <code>50%</code>, <code>auto</code>, <code>min-content</code> needed a box to measure against; now it exists, so they resolve. <a href="#style-recalc">Style Recalc</a> gave the <em>computed value</em> (<code>50%</code>); Layout makes it the <em>used value</em> (<code>400px</code> inside an 800px parent).</p>
<p>Layout is expensive. Inserting a DOM node triggers it. Changing <code>font-size</code> triggers it. Resizing the window triggers it. Reading <code>getBoundingClientRect</code> mid-animation can trigger it repeatedly.</p>
<p>That's why <a href="#uselayouteffect"><code>useLayoutEffect</code></a> sits where it does, back in section III: right after the DOM write and before the paint. Any reads there force one layout, and any correction you make lands before the user sees the first frame.</p>
<h2>VII. Paint</h2>
<p>Paint doesn't fill pixels yet. As <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/inside-browser-part3">Inside look, part 3</a> describes it, in Chrome the main thread walks the layout tree and writes down drawing instructions, called paint records: "background first, then text, then border". Raster threads later turn those records into pixels, tile by tile.</p>
<p>The browser splits the page into a few layers, images drawn separately and stacked at the end. Most elements share a layer with the elements around them, and an element's <code>background</code>, <code>color</code>, <code>box-shadow</code> and <code>border</code> are all drawn into that shared layer. Only a few elements get a layer of their own, for example one with <code>will-change: transform</code>.</p>
<p><strong>Used → actual.</strong> The last of the six value stages. Some used values can't be drawn exactly. The example in <a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/css-cascade-5/#actual">CSS Cascade 5 §4.6</a>: a device may only draw borders in whole pixels, so the browser approximates a fractional border width. (Unrelated to CSS <code>transform: translate()</code>, which lives in the next section.)</p>
<p>Paint records are made on the main thread, the same thread that runs your JavaScript.</p>
<h2>VIII. Composite</h2>
<p>The compositor thread takes the layers, places them, and sends a frame to the GPU, which draws it on screen.</p>
<p><code>transform</code> and <code>opacity</code> live here. Measured three times on headless Chrome 156, recording a one-second trace each time: a CSS animation that only changes <code>transform</code> triggered no style recalc, no layout and no paint on the main thread. The same animation on <code>left</code> or <code>width</code> ran layout and paint once in every frame, about 60 times in that second (57 to 61). Moving an element by setting <code>transform</code> from JavaScript every frame still ran style recalc each frame, but no layout or paint.</p>
<p>So CSS animations on <code>transform</code> or <code>opacity</code> keep moving while the main thread is busy: per <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/inside-browser-part3">Inside look, part 3</a>, the compositor thread doesn't wait on JavaScript or style calculation. Animations on <code>left</code>, <code>top</code>, or <code>width</code> need layout and paint on the main thread every frame. When JavaScript keeps that thread busy, frames are dropped and the animation stutters.</p>
<h2>IX. useEffect</h2>
<p><code>useEffect</code> usually fires after the browser has painted. React's docs say "generally", and the exceptions matter:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Click, keydown, and other discrete input.</strong> The <a href="https://react.dev/blog/2022/03/08/react-18-upgrade-guide">React 18 upgrade guide</a> says React 18 and later run <code>useEffect</code> before the paint. On headless Chrome 156, after a click, both React 18.3.1 and 19.3.1 ran <code>useEffect</code> before that frame's paint. That is the effect function itself. A render started by a <code>setState</code> inside it landed after the paint in all 10 runs of the tooltip test in section III.</li>
<li><strong>Anything else: a timer, a network response.</strong> React generally lets the browser paint first, but doesn't promise it. Also on Chrome 156, a <code>setTimeout</code> update ran <code>useEffect</code> after the paint in React 19.3.1, and before the next frame in React 18.3.1 (3 of 3 runs).</li>
<li><strong>A state update inside <code>useLayoutEffect</code>.</strong> According to <a href="https://react.dev/reference/react/useLayoutEffect">react.dev</a>, React then runs all pending effects immediately, <code>useEffect</code> included.</li>
</ul>
<p>So <code>useEffect</code> can run before or after paint, and even when it runs before, a <code>setState</code> inside it may not make this paint. It is for work that can happen a little earlier or later without mattering: data fetches, subscriptions, event listeners. In the search box, that's the request for results from the server. Work that must happen before paint goes in <code>useLayoutEffect</code>. As <a href="https://react.dev/reference/react/useEffect">react.dev</a> notes, work that must wait until after paint, such as an <code>alert()</code>, needs a <code>setTimeout</code>.</p>
<p>Say the search box has a Clear button that empties the results and then shows an <code>alert</code> saying they were cleared. That update comes from a click, so the <code>useEffect</code> may run before paint. Call <code>alert()</code> directly there and the dialog can appear while the old list is still on screen. And because <code>alert</code> blocks the main thread, the list doesn't disappear until the user presses OK:</p>

<p><code>setTimeout</code> moves the <code>alert</code> to a later task, and the browser usually finishes painting the current frame before running it.</p>
<h2>The naming collision</h2>
<p>"Render" means two different things in frontend, and conflating them causes confusion in every performance discussion.</p>

















<table><thead><tr><th>Term</th><th>What it means</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>React render phase</td><td>Runs the component function, produces a Virtual DOM. The browser is not involved.</td></tr><tr><td>Browser Render Tree</td><td>DOM + CSSOM merged. Built from the real DOM React wrote in the commit phase.</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>React's render phase produces JavaScript objects. The browser's Render Tree is built from real DOM nodes. They don't overlap. For a given update, React finishes render and commit before the browser builds a Render Tree from the new DOM. A transition render can pause midway, and the browser keeps showing frames of the old DOM in the meantime.</p>
<h2>The full sequence</h2>
<p>Does a slow stylesheet delay React's start too? If the React bundle loads with <code>defer</code> or <code>type="module"</code>, yes: if the CSS arrives 1.5 s late, React starts running 1.5 s late. With <code>async</code>, no: the script runs as soon as it downloads, without waiting for the CSS. The <code>index.html</code> from Vite 7.3.7's <code>vite build</code> uses <code>type="module"</code>; this site's pages, built with the Next.js 15.5.12 App Router, use <code>async</code>.</p>
<p>To check this on headless Chrome 156, the server held the stylesheet back for 1.5 s but returned the script file right away, and the page recorded when the script started running and when the first frame (first contentful paint) was drawn. The script was downloaded early, so if it still ran only at 1.5 s, it was waiting for the CSS. Three runs per page, plus three more for <code>defer</code> and <code>type="module"</code> with the script moved before the <code>&#x3C;link></code>:</p>



































<table><thead><tr><th>Script on the page</th><th>Script runs at</th><th><code>DOMContentLoaded</code></th><th>First frame</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>none</td><td>—</td><td>6 to 8 ms</td><td>1528 to 1536 ms</td></tr><tr><td><code>defer</code></td><td>1511 to 1522 ms</td><td>same time as the script</td><td>1520 to 1532 ms</td></tr><tr><td><code>type="module"</code></td><td>1508 to 1516 ms</td><td>same time as the script</td><td>1516 to 1528 ms</td></tr><tr><td><code>async</code></td><td>8 to 11 ms</td><td>6 to 9 ms</td><td>1520 to 1532 ms</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>For <code>defer</code> and <code>type="module"</code>, it made no difference whether the script tag came before or after the <code>&#x3C;link></code>. Per the HTML spec's <a href="https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html#the-end">"The end"</a> section, once parsing ends, a deferred script waits while any stylesheet the parser has seen is still loading, including one written after the script. An <code>async</code> script isn't part of that step, so it doesn't wait.</p>
<p><code>async</code> only lets React's code start earlier, though. The script ran at 8 to 11 ms, but the browser doesn't paint while the stylesheet is missing. The last column is measured: with <code>async</code>, the first frame still appeared only at 1520 to 1532 ms, about the same as with <code>defer</code>.</p>
<pre><code>Browser receives HTML
  │
  ├── HTML parser ──► DOM
  │                    │
  │                    ├──► React bundle runs            ← defer / module: waits for every stylesheet in the page
  │                    │                                    async: runs once downloaded, no wait for CSS
  │                    │       → createRoot(#root).render(&#x3C;App />)
  │                    │       → render + commit        React writes DOM nodes (the app is live from here)
  │                    ├──► DOMContentLoaded             ← DOM parsed + defer/module scripts done
  │                    │
  └── CSS fetch ──► CSSOM
                       │
      DOM + CSSOM ─────┴──► Render Tree ──► Layout ──► Paint ──► Composite ──► First Contentful Paint
                            ↑ only once the CSS is in, even if an async React already rendered

  scripts   &#x3C;script>               blocks the parser; waits for earlier stylesheets, then runs
            &#x3C;script defer>         parallel fetch; runs after parsing, once every stylesheet is in
            &#x3C;script async>         parallel fetch; runs as soon as it downloads
            &#x3C;script type="module"> deferred like defer, with its own scope

window.onload      ← images, fonts, iframes all loaded; the app is usually running well before this

──────────────── every update after that ────────────────────────

any setState (event handler, fetch, timer, WebSocket...)
  → setState called
      ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │  render phase     VDOM diff; only transitions    │
      │                   can be interrupted             │
      │  commit phase     writes to real DOM             │
      │  useLayoutEffect  read layout, blocks paint      │
      │  Style Recalc     cascade, specificity, compute  │
      │  Render Tree      DOM + computed styles merged   │
      │  Layout / Reflow  geometry: position, size       │
      │  Paint            paint records per layer        │
      │  Composite        layers → GPU → screen          │
      │  useEffect        side effects (before paint     │
      │                   after a click)                 │
      └────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                               │ any setState
                               └──► back to render phase
</code></pre>
<blockquote>
<p><strong>The three paint metrics.</strong> The bootstrap path above ends at <em>FCP</em> (First Contentful Paint), the first text or image pixels from the DOM. Two cousins sit near it: <em>FP</em> (First Paint), as <a href="https://w3c.github.io/paint-timing/">Paint Timing</a> defines it, is the first pixels of anything, a non-default background counts; <em>LCP</em> (Largest Contentful Paint), per <a href="https://web.dev/articles/lcp">web.dev</a>, is when the largest image, text block or video in the viewport renders. If that largest element is an image, LCP has to wait until the image downloads.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>The loop runs for as long as the app is alive. To see how those nine steps spread across processes and threads in real time, here is the same loop laid out as a timeline:</p>

You call `setState`, and the screen does not change on that line. What you've done is schedule a rerender. React runs it, writes the result into the DOM, and the browser still has to turn that DOM into pixels before anything changes on screen.

Take a search box. You type "a". The input should show "a", and the result list below it should filter down. Between your keystroke and those pixels there are nine steps. React owns the first three and the last; the browser owns the five in the middle, the same work it does with or without a framework.

```
setState
  → render           ┐
  → commit           │  React
  → useLayoutEffect  ┘
  → Style Recalc     ┐
  → Render Tree      │
  → Layout           │  browser
  → Paint            │
  → Composite        ┘
  → useEffect           React (usually here; section IX has the exceptions)
```

## I. The render phase

React calls your component function again. The function returns a new tree of plain JavaScript objects, often called the Virtual DOM. The browser has no idea this tree exists. It's just memory.

React compares the new tree against the previous one. Two rules govern the diff:

- Different element type at the same spot (a `<div>` became a `<section>`)? Tear down the old subtree, build a new one.
- List items? The `key` prop tells React which item is which across renders.

Since React 18, this phase can be paused and restarted. With `startTransition`, you mark an update as low priority. According to [react.dev](https://react.dev/reference/react/useTransition), if a more urgent update arrives before that render finishes, React drops the partial render, handles the urgent update, and then starts the low-priority render again. Nothing has touched the DOM yet, so throwing away the unfinished work is safe.

```jsx
const [input, setInput] = useState('')
const [query, setQuery] = useState('')

function handleChange(e) {
  setInput(e.target.value)           // high priority. update input immediately

  startTransition(() => {
    setQuery(e.target.value)         // low priority. React can interrupt this render
  })
}

// <ExpensiveList> rerenders with query.
// If the user types again before it finishes, React drops
// the ongoing render and restarts with the latest query.
```

Without `startTransition`, an update from a keystroke renders synchronously in one go. The input lags until the list finishes.

## II. The commit phase

The diff is ready: in the search box, the input's value changes to "a", and a dozen list items get removed. React writes those changes to the real DOM.

This phase cannot be interrupted. Once the DOM starts changing, stopping halfway would leave a half-updated page on screen, so React runs it to completion.

Internally, in [`ReactFiberCommitWork.js`](https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberCommitWork.js), commit runs three stages:

- **Before mutation**: read what the DOM looks like before it changes. Class components use `getSnapshotBeforeUpdate` here to record things like scroll position.
- **Mutation**: actual DOM writes. `insertBefore`, `removeChild`, `setAttribute`. Old refs are detached and the previous `useLayoutEffect` cleanups run here.
- **Layout**: attach the new refs, fire `useLayoutEffect`. So "useLayoutEffect runs after commit" really means it runs inside the last of these three.

<span id="uselayouteffect"></span>

## III. useLayoutEffect

Before the browser paints anything, React fires `useLayoutEffect` synchronously.

A tooltip shows why this matters. It should sit below its button, unless there's no room below, in which case it flips above. You can't know that until the tooltip is in the DOM and you measure its height. `useLayoutEffect` is the last moment to measure (`getBoundingClientRect`, `offsetHeight`, scroll position) and fix the DOM before the user sees anything. As [react.dev](https://react.dev/reference/react/useLayoutEffect) points out, if you measure in `useEffect` instead and then set state to move the tooltip, the browser may already have painted it in the wrong place, and the user sees it jump.

A tooltip opened by a click jumps too. Tested on headless Chrome 156: click a button, the tooltip renders below it, `useEffect` measures its height and calls `setState` to flip it above. In both React 18.3.1 and 19.3.1, 10 of 10 runs painted a frame with the tooltip below before it moved. With `useLayoutEffect`, all 10 painted it above from the first frame.

After a click, `useEffect` itself does run before the paint (section IX measures it). So why the jump? The effect running early doesn't mean the render its `setState` starts also finishes before the paint. React gives updates a priority, and a click's update is the highest, so React renders it right away. In the source of both 18.3.1 and 19.3.1, an update scheduled inside an effect after a click gets `DefaultEventPriority`, lower than the click. React doesn't render a default-priority update right away; it hands it to its Scheduler, which runs it in a separate task. React doesn't promise that task comes before the browser's next paint, and in all 10 runs the paint came first.

Reading layout is **synchronous and blocking**, for every entry on the [list of properties that force layout](https://gist.github.com/paulirish/5d52fb081b3570c81e3a): `getBoundingClientRect()` computes style and layout on that line, no Promise, no `await` to warn you. A read forces that compute only when layout is *dirty*, and a **write** dirties it. One read is one pass:

```
read → style recalc → layout
```

Interleave writes and each one re-dirties, so the pass runs again and again (**layout thrashing**):

```
read → style recalc → layout → write → style recalc → layout → write → style recalc → layout
```

Fix: batch all reads, then all writes. For pure measurement, `ResizeObserver` / `IntersectionObserver` report asynchronously, no forced layout.

Commit just wrote to the DOM, so layout is dirty when `useLayoutEffect` starts. The first read inside it runs Style Recalc, Render Tree and Layout right there, before the call returns. In that case sections IV to VI happen early, inside the effect, and the browser reuses the result unless the effect writes again. A trace recorded on headless Chrome 156, writing to the DOM and then calling `getBoundingClientRect()` once, shows 16 nested events between the call and its return, the same 16 in each of three runs. Among them, in order, are `Document::recalcStyle`, `Document::rebuildLayoutTree` and `Layout`, one for each of those sections; the rest are wrappers such as `Document::UpdateStyleAndLayout` and finer steps inside them.

`useLayoutEffect` blocks the paint. Keep it fast.

Now the browser takes over.

> **CRP, technically.** People call this whole pipeline (Style Recalc through Composite) the Critical Rendering Path. Strictly, by [web.dev](https://web.dev/learn/performance/understanding-the-critical-path)'s definition, CRP is the path to the *first* render of a page. After that, `setState` reuses the same steps, but it isn't CRP anymore: CRP is about which resources (HTML, CSS, parser-blocking scripts) the first render has to wait for.

<span id="style-recalc"></span>

## IV. Style Recalc

The DOM changed, so the browser has to work out what every affected element should look like. In the terms of [CSS Cascade 5 §4](https://www.w3.org/TR/css-cascade-5/#value-stages), one property value on one element moves through six stages before it reaches the screen:

```
declared → cascaded → specified → computed → used → actual
```

Style Recalc runs the first four (the steps below). *Used* and *actual* finish later, in Layout and Paint.

**Collecting.** The browser gathers styles from three sources: its own builtin defaults (User Agent), any preferences the user has configured in their browser, and your stylesheet (Author).

**Cascading.** All collected declarations compete. The browser resolves conflicts in the order [CSS Cascade 5 §6.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/css-cascade-5/#cascade-sort) gives, highest priority first:

1. Transitions
2. User Agent + `!important`
3. User + `!important`
4. Author + `!important`
5. Animations
6. Author
7. User
8. User Agent

Within the same origin and importance, the `style` attribute beats any stylesheet rule. Next come cascade layers (`@layer`); after that, specificity: IDs beat classes, classes beat type selectors. If specificity is equal, the declaration that appears last wins. The reference below gives example selectors and their scores. It puts the `style` attribute and `!important` on the same scale, as 1-0-0-0 and 1-0-0-0-0; that is a memory aid, since in the spec neither is part of specificity.

<iframe src="https://specificity.webcore.io/" width="100%" height="800" style="border:none; margin: 24px 0;" title="CSS Specificity Reference"></iframe>

**Defaulting.** Properties with no declared value still need one. Two ways to fill it:  
Text-ish properties inherit from the parent: `color`, `font-size`, `font-family`.  
Box-ish properties fall back to a spec default: `border-style` → `none`, `margin` → `0`.  
Override either path with `inherit`, `initial`, `unset`, or `revert`.

**Resolving (the easy half).** First of two passes ([section VI](#layout-reflow) is the other). Anything that doesn't need geometry becomes concrete. `em` resolves against the element's own font size (`padding: 1em` on a 20px element is 20px); only inside `font-size` itself does it use the parent's. `rem` resolves against the root, `bold` becomes `700`, relative paths become absolute URLs. Anything that needs the box size (`50%`, `auto`, `min-content`) can't resolve yet, so it waits for Layout.

Output: every node's *computed style*. Note *computed*: `width: 50%` is still `50%` here, not a pixel. You can see this from JavaScript: on an element with `display: none` (no box, no layout), `getComputedStyle(el).width` returns `50%`. Show the element and the same call returns `400px`, because for laid-out elements it reports the value after Layout.

## V. Render Tree

DOM plus computed styles merge into the Render Tree (Chrome calls it the layout tree). It's the DOM with style attached, minus the nodes that take up no space, plus a few that aren't in the DOM at all.

`display: none`: excluded. No node in the tree, no space in the layout.  
`visibility: hidden`: included. Space reserved, pixels not drawn.  
`<title>`, `<head>`, `<script>`: excluded, because the browser's default stylesheet gives them `display: none`.  
`::before` / `::after` with `content`: included. [Inside look, part 3](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/inside-browser-part3) notes they go into the layout tree even though they're not DOM nodes.

<span id="layout-reflow"></span>

## VI. Layout / Reflow

The browser walks the Render Tree and calculates the geometry of every element: position, width, height. This step is also called Reflow. In the search box, the list just lost a dozen items, so its height shrinks and everything below it moves up. Two CSS steps finish here:

**Formatting.** The browser organizes elements into formatting contexts: block, inline, flex, grid. Each context has rules for how its children stack and flow.

**Resolving (the layout half).** The second pass. `50%`, `auto`, `min-content` needed a box to measure against; now it exists, so they resolve. [Style Recalc](#style-recalc) gave the *computed value* (`50%`); Layout makes it the *used value* (`400px` inside an 800px parent).

Layout is expensive. Inserting a DOM node triggers it. Changing `font-size` triggers it. Resizing the window triggers it. Reading `getBoundingClientRect` mid-animation can trigger it repeatedly.

That's why [`useLayoutEffect`](#uselayouteffect) sits where it does, back in section III: right after the DOM write and before the paint. Any reads there force one layout, and any correction you make lands before the user sees the first frame.

## VII. Paint

Paint doesn't fill pixels yet. As [Inside look, part 3](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/inside-browser-part3) describes it, in Chrome the main thread walks the layout tree and writes down drawing instructions, called paint records: "background first, then text, then border". Raster threads later turn those records into pixels, tile by tile.

The browser splits the page into a few layers, images drawn separately and stacked at the end. Most elements share a layer with the elements around them, and an element's `background`, `color`, `box-shadow` and `border` are all drawn into that shared layer. Only a few elements get a layer of their own, for example one with `will-change: transform`.

**Used → actual.** The last of the six value stages. Some used values can't be drawn exactly. The example in [CSS Cascade 5 §4.6](https://www.w3.org/TR/css-cascade-5/#actual): a device may only draw borders in whole pixels, so the browser approximates a fractional border width. (Unrelated to CSS `transform: translate()`, which lives in the next section.)

Paint records are made on the main thread, the same thread that runs your JavaScript.

## VIII. Composite

The compositor thread takes the layers, places them, and sends a frame to the GPU, which draws it on screen.

`transform` and `opacity` live here. Measured three times on headless Chrome 156, recording a one-second trace each time: a CSS animation that only changes `transform` triggered no style recalc, no layout and no paint on the main thread. The same animation on `left` or `width` ran layout and paint once in every frame, about 60 times in that second (57 to 61). Moving an element by setting `transform` from JavaScript every frame still ran style recalc each frame, but no layout or paint.

So CSS animations on `transform` or `opacity` keep moving while the main thread is busy: per [Inside look, part 3](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/inside-browser-part3), the compositor thread doesn't wait on JavaScript or style calculation. Animations on `left`, `top`, or `width` need layout and paint on the main thread every frame. When JavaScript keeps that thread busy, frames are dropped and the animation stutters.

## IX. useEffect

`useEffect` usually fires after the browser has painted. React's docs say "generally", and the exceptions matter:

- **Click, keydown, and other discrete input.** The [React 18 upgrade guide](https://react.dev/blog/2022/03/08/react-18-upgrade-guide) says React 18 and later run `useEffect` before the paint. On headless Chrome 156, after a click, both React 18.3.1 and 19.3.1 ran `useEffect` before that frame's paint. That is the effect function itself. A render started by a `setState` inside it landed after the paint in all 10 runs of the tooltip test in section III.
- **Anything else: a timer, a network response.** React generally lets the browser paint first, but doesn't promise it. Also on Chrome 156, a `setTimeout` update ran `useEffect` after the paint in React 19.3.1, and before the next frame in React 18.3.1 (3 of 3 runs).
- **A state update inside `useLayoutEffect`.** According to [react.dev](https://react.dev/reference/react/useLayoutEffect), React then runs all pending effects immediately, `useEffect` included.

So `useEffect` can run before or after paint, and even when it runs before, a `setState` inside it may not make this paint. It is for work that can happen a little earlier or later without mattering: data fetches, subscriptions, event listeners. In the search box, that's the request for results from the server. Work that must happen before paint goes in `useLayoutEffect`. As [react.dev](https://react.dev/reference/react/useEffect) notes, work that must wait until after paint, such as an `alert()`, needs a `setTimeout`.

Say the search box has a Clear button that empties the results and then shows an `alert` saying they were cleared. That update comes from a click, so the `useEffect` may run before paint. Call `alert()` directly there and the dialog can appear while the old list is still on screen. And because `alert` blocks the main thread, the list doesn't disappear until the user presses OK:

```js
function handleClear() {
  setResults([]);
  setCleared(true);
}

useEffect(() => {
  if (!cleared) return;
  // alert('Cleared'); // may show before the list disappears
  const id = setTimeout(() => alert('Cleared'), 0);
  return () => clearTimeout(id);
}, [cleared]);
```

`setTimeout` moves the `alert` to a later task, and the browser usually finishes painting the current frame before running it.

## The naming collision

"Render" means two different things in frontend, and conflating them causes confusion in every performance discussion.

| Term | What it means |
|---|---|
| React render phase | Runs the component function, produces a Virtual DOM. The browser is not involved. |
| Browser Render Tree | DOM + CSSOM merged. Built from the real DOM React wrote in the commit phase. |

React's render phase produces JavaScript objects. The browser's Render Tree is built from real DOM nodes. They don't overlap. For a given update, React finishes render and commit before the browser builds a Render Tree from the new DOM. A transition render can pause midway, and the browser keeps showing frames of the old DOM in the meantime.

## The full sequence

Does a slow stylesheet delay React's start too? If the React bundle loads with `defer` or `type="module"`, yes: if the CSS arrives 1.5 s late, React starts running 1.5 s late. With `async`, no: the script runs as soon as it downloads, without waiting for the CSS. The `index.html` from Vite 7.3.7's `vite build` uses `type="module"`; this site's pages, built with the Next.js 15.5.12 App Router, use `async`.

To check this on headless Chrome 156, the server held the stylesheet back for 1.5 s but returned the script file right away, and the page recorded when the script started running and when the first frame (first contentful paint) was drawn. The script was downloaded early, so if it still ran only at 1.5 s, it was waiting for the CSS. Three runs per page, plus three more for `defer` and `type="module"` with the script moved before the `<link>`:

| Script on the page | Script runs at | `DOMContentLoaded` | First frame |
|---|---|---|---|
| none | — | 6 to 8 ms | 1528 to 1536 ms |
| `defer` | 1511 to 1522 ms | same time as the script | 1520 to 1532 ms |
| `type="module"` | 1508 to 1516 ms | same time as the script | 1516 to 1528 ms |
| `async` | 8 to 11 ms | 6 to 9 ms | 1520 to 1532 ms |

For `defer` and `type="module"`, it made no difference whether the script tag came before or after the `<link>`. Per the HTML spec's ["The end"](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html#the-end) section, once parsing ends, a deferred script waits while any stylesheet the parser has seen is still loading, including one written after the script. An `async` script isn't part of that step, so it doesn't wait.

`async` only lets React's code start earlier, though. The script ran at 8 to 11 ms, but the browser doesn't paint while the stylesheet is missing. The last column is measured: with `async`, the first frame still appeared only at 1520 to 1532 ms, about the same as with `defer`.

```
Browser receives HTML
  │
  ├── HTML parser ──► DOM
  │                    │
  │                    ├──► React bundle runs            ← defer / module: waits for every stylesheet in the page
  │                    │                                    async: runs once downloaded, no wait for CSS
  │                    │       → createRoot(#root).render(<App />)
  │                    │       → render + commit        React writes DOM nodes (the app is live from here)
  │                    ├──► DOMContentLoaded             ← DOM parsed + defer/module scripts done
  │                    │
  └── CSS fetch ──► CSSOM
                       │
      DOM + CSSOM ─────┴──► Render Tree ──► Layout ──► Paint ──► Composite ──► First Contentful Paint
                            ↑ only once the CSS is in, even if an async React already rendered

  scripts   <script>               blocks the parser; waits for earlier stylesheets, then runs
            <script defer>         parallel fetch; runs after parsing, once every stylesheet is in
            <script async>         parallel fetch; runs as soon as it downloads
            <script type="module"> deferred like defer, with its own scope

window.onload      ← images, fonts, iframes all loaded; the app is usually running well before this

──────────────── every update after that ────────────────────────

any setState (event handler, fetch, timer, WebSocket...)
  → setState called
      ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │  render phase     VDOM diff; only transitions    │
      │                   can be interrupted             │
      │  commit phase     writes to real DOM             │
      │  useLayoutEffect  read layout, blocks paint      │
      │  Style Recalc     cascade, specificity, compute  │
      │  Render Tree      DOM + computed styles merged   │
      │  Layout / Reflow  geometry: position, size       │
      │  Paint            paint records per layer        │
      │  Composite        layers → GPU → screen          │
      │  useEffect        side effects (before paint     │
      │                   after a click)                 │
      └────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                               │ any setState
                               └──► back to render phase
```

> **The three paint metrics.** The bootstrap path above ends at *FCP* (First Contentful Paint), the first text or image pixels from the DOM. Two cousins sit near it: *FP* (First Paint), as [Paint Timing](https://w3c.github.io/paint-timing/) defines it, is the first pixels of anything, a non-default background counts; *LCP* (Largest Contentful Paint), per [web.dev](https://web.dev/articles/lcp), is when the largest image, text block or video in the viewport renders. If that largest element is an image, LCP has to wait until the image downloads.

The loop runs for as long as the app is alive. To see how those nine steps spread across processes and threads in real time, here is the same loop laid out as a timeline:

## References

**React internals**

- [Inside React's FiberWorkLoop](/v2/inside-react-fiberworkloop). Follow up post of mine. Zooms inside the "render phase" and "commit phase" bullets above, walking through the four numbered stages of React's internal reconciler workloop.
- [React 技术揭秘](https://react.iamkasong.com) by 卡颂 (KaSong). A simplified Chinese deep dive into Fiber, Scheduler, Lanes, and Hooks. The standard narrative reference for React at source level. Source on GitHub: [BetaSu/just-react](https://github.com/BetaSu/just-react).
- [图解React: reconciler 运作流程](https://7km.top/main/reconciler-workflow). Another simplified Chinese resource, but function by function. Traces the reconciler in four steps from `scheduleUpdateOnFiber` to `commitRoot`, with a diagram of the call graph. Complements KaSong's book with a more concrete workflow.
- [A Cartoon Intro to Fiber](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZCuYPiUIONs) by Lin Clark, React Conf 2017. Visual walkthrough of why Fiber replaced the old stack reconciler.

**Browser rendering pipeline**

- [Inside look at modern web browser](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/inside-browser-part1/) by Mariko Kosaka. Four part series on how Chrome's processes and threads cooperate.
- [How browsers work](https://web.dev/articles/howbrowserswork) by Tali Garsiel and Paul Irish. The long form classic on what happens from bytes to pixels.
- [How web browsers work: the render tree (part 7)](https://dev.to/arikaturika/how-web-browsers-work-the-render-tree-part-7-with-illustrations-24h3) by Arika O. Part 7 of an illustrated dev.to series. Walks render tree construction step by step with diagrams.
- [The Anatomy of Browser Rendering](https://medium.com/@regondaakhil/the-anatomy-of-browser-rendering-how-web-pages-come-to-life-6fa9e801a3f) by Akhil Regonda. Six step walkthrough from parse to composite, with optimization notes along the way.
- [浏览器是如何渲染网页的？](https://juejin.cn/post/6952878811046215711), Kerb's simplified Chinese translation of an article by Uday Hiwarale. Covers DOM, CSSOM, and render tree, and how render-blocking CSS and parser-blocking scripts reshape the pipeline.

**Critical Rendering Path**

- [Render Tree Construction](https://web.dev/articles/critical-rendering-path/render-tree-construction) by Ilya Grigorik. How DOM and CSSOM merge, what gets included, what gets dropped.
- [Measure the Critical Rendering Path](https://web.dev/articles/critical-rendering-path/measure-crp) by Ilya Grigorik. How to measure CRP timing with the Navigation Timing API and Lighthouse, and why DevTools alone is a poor fit for it.

**Layout and reflow**

- [On Layout & Web Performance](https://kellegous.com/j/2013/01/26/layout-performance/) by Kelly Norton. The classic post on layout thrashing. Browsers compute layout lazily, so read-write-read forces reflow every time.
- [Avoid large, complex layouts and layout thrashing](https://web.dev/articles/avoid-large-complex-layouts-and-layout-thrashing) by Jeremy Wagner, Paul Lewis, Barry Pollard. Concrete techniques: batch reads before writes, avoid forced synchronous layout, keep the DOM small.
- [What is DOM reflow?](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/27637184/what-is-dom-reflow/27637245#27637245) Stack Overflow thread. Short canonical answer for what reflow is and what triggers it.
- [Browser Rendering Optimization](https://github.com/vasanthk/browser-rendering-optimization/blob/master/README.md) by Vasanth Krishnamoorthy. Notes from Paul Lewis and Cameron Pittman's Udacity course on hitting 60fps. Covers pipeline stages, frame budget, and per step optimizations.

**Extensibility**

- [Houdini APIs](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Houdini_APIs) on MDN. Houdini opens the CSS engine's internal steps to userland. The Paint, Layout, and Animation Worklets would each hook into one step of the pipeline above, but only the Paint Worklet has shipped, in Chrome and Edge. Other Houdini parts, such as `@property`, work in Firefox and Safari too.
- [Web Workers vs Service Workers vs Worklets](https://bitsofco.de/web-workers-vs-service-workers-vs-worklets/) by Ire Aderinokun. Short comparison of what each one does; of the three, Worklets are the ones that hook into the rendering pipeline.

<h2>一、render 階段</h2>
<p>React 重新呼叫一次元件的 function。這個 function 回傳一棵由普通 JavaScript 物件組成的新樹，一般叫它 Virtual DOM。瀏覽器碰不到這棵樹，它只是記憶體裡的資料。</p>
<p>React 拿新樹跟上一次的樹比對，比對時照兩條規則：</p>
<ul>
<li>同一個位置的元素類型變了，例如 <code>&#x3C;div></code> 變成 <code>&#x3C;section></code>，就把舊的整棵子樹拆掉，重新建一棵。</li>
<li>清單裡的項目，React 靠 <code>key</code> 這個 prop 認出前後兩次 render 裡哪個項目是哪個。</li>
</ul>
<p>React 18 開始，這個階段可以暫停、也可以重來。用 <code>startTransition</code> 包起來的更新，priority 會被標低。照 <a href="https://react.dev/reference/react/useTransition">react.dev</a> 的說明，如果這次 render 做到一半，來了一個比較急的更新，React 會丟掉做到一半的結果，先處理急的那個，之後再從頭跑一次 priority 低的那個 render。因為這時候 DOM 一個字都還沒動，丟掉做到一半的結果也不會出事。</p>

<p>沒有 <code>startTransition</code> 的話，按鍵觸發的更新會一口氣同步 render 完，清單 render 完之前，輸入框都會卡著。</p>
<h2>二、commit 階段</h2>
<p>比對的結果出來了。以搜尋框為例，輸入框的值要改成「a」，清單要拿掉十幾個項目。React 把這些變更寫進真正的 DOM。</p>
<p>這個階段不能中斷。DOM 一旦開始改，中途停下來的話，畫面上就會出現改到一半的頁面，所以 React 會一口氣做完。</p>
<p>在 <a href="https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberCommitWork.js"><code>ReactFiberCommitWork.js</code></a> 裡，React 把 commit 分成三段：</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Before mutation</strong>：在 DOM 改動之前，先記下現在的狀態。class 元件的 <code>getSnapshotBeforeUpdate</code> 在這裡跑，常拿來記下捲動位置。</li>
<li><strong>Mutation</strong>：真的寫 DOM，<code>insertBefore</code>、<code>removeChild</code>、<code>setAttribute</code> 都在這段。舊的 ref 在這段解除，上一次 <code>useLayoutEffect</code> 的 cleanup 也在這段跑。</li>
<li><strong>Layout</strong>：接上新的 ref，然後執行 <code>useLayoutEffect</code>。所以常聽到的「<code>useLayoutEffect</code> 在 commit 之後執行」，實際上是在這三段的最後一段裡執行。</li>
</ul>
<p><span id="uselayouteffect"></span></p>
<h2>三、useLayoutEffect</h2>
<p>瀏覽器畫出任何東西之前，React 會同步執行 <code>useLayoutEffect</code>。</p>
<p>拿 tooltip 來看為什麼需要這一步。tooltip 平常放在按鈕下方，如果下方空間不夠，就要改放到上方。可是 tooltip 要先放進 DOM、量過高度，才知道下方夠不夠放。要量尺寸（<code>getBoundingClientRect</code>、<code>offsetHeight</code>、捲動位置）、再趕在使用者看到之前把 DOM 改對，<code>useLayoutEffect</code> 是最後的機會。<a href="https://react.dev/reference/react/useLayoutEffect">react.dev</a> 提到，如果改在 <code>useEffect</code> 裡量，再用 setState 把 tooltip 移過去，瀏覽器可能已經把放錯位置的 tooltip 畫出來了，使用者會看到它跳一下。</p>
<p>點一下才打開的 tooltip 也會跳。在 headless Chrome 156 上用一個 tooltip 測試：點按鈕打開，先畫在按鈕下方，<code>useEffect</code> 量完高度再 setState 把它翻到上方。React 18.3.1 跟 19.3.1 各跑 10 次，10 次都是先在下方畫出一個 frame，才跳到上方。改用 <code>useLayoutEffect</code>，10 次都直接畫在上方。</p>
<p>點擊觸發的更新，<code>useEffect</code> 其實會在 paint 之前執行，第九節有實測。那 tooltip 為什麼還會跳？effect 在 paint 之前跑完，不代表 effect 裡 setState 排的那次 render 也會在 paint 之前做完。React 的更新分 priority，點擊觸發的更新 priority 最高，React 會馬上 render。effect 執行時排的更新就不一樣了。照 React 18.3.1 跟 19.3.1 的原始碼，點擊之後在 effect 裡排的更新，priority 是 default（<code>DefaultEventPriority</code>），比點擊低。default priority 的更新 React 不馬上做，而是交給它的 Scheduler，在另一個 task 裡跑。React 沒有保證這個 task 會排在瀏覽器下一次 paint 之前。上面的測試 10 次都是 paint 先，所以 tooltip 第一個畫出來的 frame 還在下方。</p>
<p>讀 layout 是<strong>同步</strong>的，會卡住 main thread，<a href="https://gist.github.com/paulirish/5d52fb081b3570c81e3a">會強制 layout 的屬性清單</a>裡的每一個都是這樣。<code>getBoundingClientRect()</code> 執行的那一行，瀏覽器就在算 style 跟 layout，沒有 Promise，也沒有 <code>await</code> 提醒。不過只有 layout 是 <em>dirty</em>（過期、需要重算）的時候，讀取才會觸發重算，而<strong>寫入</strong>會讓它變成 dirty。讀一次就是算一輪：</p>
<pre><code>讀取 → style recalc → layout
</code></pre>
<p>讀跟寫交錯的話，每寫一次 layout 就又過期，於是同樣這一輪會一直重跑，這叫 <strong>layout thrashing</strong>：</p>
<pre><code>讀取 → style recalc → layout → 寫入 → style recalc → layout → 寫入 → style recalc → layout
</code></pre>
<p>解法是先把要讀的全部讀完，再一次寫。如果只是要量尺寸，<code>ResizeObserver</code>、<code>IntersectionObserver</code> 會非同步回報結果，不會強制 layout。</p>
<p>commit 剛寫過 DOM，所以 <code>useLayoutEffect</code> 開始的時候 layout 一定是 dirty 的。effect 裡第一次讀 layout，例如呼叫 <code>getBoundingClientRect()</code>，瀏覽器就當場把第四到第六節的事做完，也就是 Style Recalc、Render Tree、Layout。三步都做完，這個呼叫才回傳，effect 才接著往下跑。在 headless Chrome 156 錄的 trace 裡，寫完 DOM 之後呼叫一次 <code>getBoundingClientRect()</code>，從呼叫到回傳之間有 16 個事件，一層包一層，跑三次都是同樣這 16 個。最外層是 <code>Document::UpdateStyleAndLayout</code>，它底下依序出現 <code>Document::recalcStyle</code>、<code>Document::rebuildLayoutTree</code> 跟 <code>Layout</code>，正好對到這三步。剩下的事件是這三步外面再包的一層，或是它們裡面更細的步驟，例如 <code>Layout</code> 裡面的 <code>LocalFrameView::performLayout</code>。effect 之後如果沒有再寫 DOM，等到要 paint 的時候，瀏覽器不用再算一次 style 跟 layout，直接用 effect 裡算好的。</p>
<p><code>useLayoutEffect</code> 會卡住 paint，所以裡面的程式要快。</p>
<p>接下來的步驟由瀏覽器做。</p>
<blockquote>
<p><strong>嚴格說起來的 CRP。</strong> 從 Style Recalc 到 Composite 這一整段，很常被叫成 Critical Rendering Path（關鍵渲染路徑）。不過照 <a href="https://web.dev/learn/performance/understanding-the-critical-path">web.dev</a> 的定義，CRP 指的是頁面<em>第一次</em> render 之前的那段路。之後每次 <code>setState</code> 也走同樣這幾步，只是那已經不叫 CRP 了，因為 CRP 關心的是第一次 render 要等哪些資源（HTML、CSS、會卡住 parser 的 script）。</p>
</blockquote>
<p><span id="style-recalc"></span></p>
<h2>四、Style Recalc</h2>
<p>DOM 變了，瀏覽器就要重新算出受影響的每個元素長什麼樣子。照 CSS 規格 <a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/css-cascade-5/#value-stages">CSS Cascade 5 §4</a> 的講法，一個元素上的一個屬性值，從寫在 CSS 裡到出現在螢幕上，要經過六種形式：</p>
<pre><code>declared → cascaded → specified → computed → used → actual
</code></pre>
<p>Style Recalc 負責前四種，也就是下面這幾步。<em>used</em> 跟 <em>actual</em> 要到 Layout 跟 Paint 才會算完。</p>
<p><strong>收集。</strong> 瀏覽器從三個地方收集 style：瀏覽器自己內建的預設值（User Agent）、使用者在瀏覽器裡設定的偏好（User），還有網站自己的 stylesheet（Author）。</p>
<p><strong>cascade。</strong> 收集到的宣告會互相競爭。發生衝突時，瀏覽器照 <a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/css-cascade-5/#cascade-sort">CSS Cascade 5 §6.1</a> 列的順序決定誰贏，越上面越優先：</p>
<ol>
<li>Transitions</li>
<li>User Agent + <code>!important</code></li>
<li>User + <code>!important</code></li>
<li>Author + <code>!important</code></li>
<li>Animations</li>
<li>Author</li>
<li>User</li>
<li>User Agent</li>
</ol>
<p>來源跟 <code>!important</code> 都一樣的時候，寫在 <code>style</code> attribute 裡的宣告會贏過任何 stylesheet 裡的規則。接著比 cascade layer（<code>@layer</code>），再來才比 specificity：ID 贏過 class，class 贏過元素名稱。specificity 也一樣的話，寫在後面的宣告贏。下面這張參考表列了一些 selector 的分數。它把 <code>style</code> attribute 跟 <code>!important</code> 也放在同一套分數上，寫成 1-0-0-0 跟 1-0-0-0-0；這只是幫忙記的寫法，規格裡這兩個都不算 specificity。</p>
<iframe src="https://specificity.webcore.io/" width="100%" height="800" style="border:none; margin: 24px 0;" title="CSS Specificity Reference"></iframe>
<p><strong>補預設值。</strong> 沒有任何宣告的屬性還是需要一個值，補法有兩種。<br>
跟文字有關的屬性從 parent 繼承，例如 <code>color</code>、<code>font-size</code>、<code>font-family</code>。<br>
跟盒子有關的屬性用規格寫好的初始值，例如 <code>border-style</code> 是 <code>none</code>、<code>margin</code> 是 <code>0</code>。<br>
這兩條路都可以用 <code>inherit</code>、<code>initial</code>、<code>unset</code> 或 <code>revert</code> 改掉。</p>
<p><strong>換算（不需要尺寸的那一半）。</strong> 換算分兩次，這是第一次，另一次在<a href="#layout-reflow">第六節</a>。不需要知道幾何尺寸的值，在這裡都換成具體的值。<code>em</code> 照元素自己的字級換算，例如字級 20px 的元素寫 <code>padding: 1em</code>，就是 20px；只有寫在 <code>font-size</code> 裡的 <code>em</code> 才照 parent 的字級算。<code>rem</code> 照根元素的字級算，<code>bold</code> 變成 <code>700</code>，相對路徑變成完整的 URL。至於要知道盒子多大才算得出來的值，像 <code>50%</code>、<code>auto</code>、<code>min-content</code>，這時還沒辦法算，要等 Layout。</p>
<p>這一步的產出是每個節點的 <em>computed style</em>。這裡說的是 <em>computed</em>，<code>width: 50%</code> 這時還是 <code>50%</code>，還不是像素。從 JavaScript 也能確認這一點。一個元素設成 <code>display: none</code>，沒有盒子、也不做 layout，<code>getComputedStyle(el).width</code> 回傳的是 <code>50%</code>。把它顯示出來，同一個呼叫就回傳 <code>400px</code>，因為元素有做 layout 的時候，這個 API 回報的是 Layout 之後的值。</p>
<h2>五、Render Tree</h2>
<p>DOM 跟 computed style 合起來，就是 Render Tree（Chrome 叫它 layout tree）。它大致就是掛上 style 的 DOM，不過拿掉了完全不佔空間的節點，又多了幾個 DOM 裡沒有的節點。</p>
<p><code>display: none</code>：不放進來。樹裡沒有這個節點，layout 也不留位置。<br>
<code>visibility: hidden</code>：放進來。位置照留，只是不畫像素。<br>
<code>&#x3C;title></code>、<code>&#x3C;head></code>、<code>&#x3C;script></code>：不放進來，因為瀏覽器內建的 stylesheet 把它們設成 <code>display: none</code>。<br>
有 <code>content</code> 的 <code>::before</code>、<code>::after</code>：放進來。<a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/inside-browser-part3">Inside look, part 3</a> 提到，它們雖然不是 DOM 節點，也會放進 layout tree。</p>
<p><span id="layout-reflow"></span></p>
<h2>六、Layout / Reflow</h2>
<p>瀏覽器走過 Render Tree，算出每個元素的幾何資訊：位置、寬、高。這一步也叫 Reflow。回到搜尋框，清單少了十幾個項目，高度變矮，清單下面的東西全部往上移，這些新位置都在這一步算出來。CSS 有兩步在這裡完成：</p>
<p><strong>排版。</strong> 瀏覽器把元素分進不同的 formatting context，像 block、inline、flex、grid。每一種 context 都有自己的規則，決定裡面的子元素怎麼堆、怎麼流動。</p>
<p><strong>換算（需要尺寸的那一半）。</strong> 第二次換算。<code>50%</code>、<code>auto</code>、<code>min-content</code> 要有一個盒子當基準才能算，現在盒子有了，就可以算出來。<a href="#style-recalc">Style Recalc</a> 給的是 <em>computed value</em>（<code>50%</code>），Layout 把它變成 <em>used value</em>（在 800px 寬的 parent 裡就是 <code>400px</code>）。</p>
<p>Layout 很花時間。插入一個 DOM 節點會觸發它，改 <code>font-size</code> 會觸發它，調整視窗大小也會觸發它。動畫進行中去讀 <code>getBoundingClientRect</code>，可能會讓它一再重跑。</p>
<p>所以 <a href="#uselayouteffect"><code>useLayoutEffect</code></a> 才排在第三節那個位置：DOM 剛寫完、還沒 paint。在那裡讀尺寸，頂多強制一次 layout，而且在那裡做的修正，會趕在使用者看到第一個畫面之前生效。</p>
<h2>七、Paint</h2>
<p>Paint 這一步其實還沒填像素。<a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/inside-browser-part3">Inside look, part 3</a> 寫到，在 Chrome 裡，main thread 走過 layout tree，寫下一份份繪製指令，叫 paint record，內容像是「先畫背景，再畫文字，再畫邊框」。之後 raster thread 才照這些指令，一塊一塊（tile）把像素畫出來。</p>
<p>瀏覽器會把頁面分成幾個 layer，可以想成分開畫、最後再疊起來的幾張圖層。大部分元素都跟周圍的元素共用一個 layer，元素的 <code>background</code>、<code>color</code>、<code>box-shadow</code>、<code>border</code> 也都畫在那個 layer 上。只有少數元素會獨立成一個 layer，例如設了 <code>will-change: transform</code> 的元素。</p>
<p><strong>used → actual。</strong> 六種形式的最後一種。有些 used value 沒辦法照原樣畫出來。<a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/css-cascade-5/#actual">CSS Cascade 5 §4.6</a> 舉的例子是：裝置可能只能畫整數像素寬的邊框，遇到帶小數的邊框寬度，瀏覽器就取一個近似值。（這跟 CSS 的 <code>transform: translate()</code> 無關，那個在下一節。）</p>
<p>paint record 是在 main thread 上產生的，跟執行 JavaScript 的是同一條 thread。</p>
<h2>八、Composite</h2>
<p>compositor thread 把這些 layer 排好位置，組成一個 frame 交給 GPU，由 GPU 畫到螢幕上。</p>
<p><code>transform</code> 跟 <code>opacity</code> 就是在這一步處理的。在 headless Chrome 156 上錄一秒的 trace，量三次：CSS 動畫只改 <code>transform</code> 的時候，main thread 上一次 style recalc、layout 或 paint 都沒有。同樣的動畫改成動 <code>left</code> 或 <code>width</code>，每個 frame 都要跑一次 layout 跟 paint，一秒下來大約 60 次（57 到 61 次）。改用 JavaScript 每個 frame 去設 <code>transform</code>，style recalc 還是每個 frame 都跑，但 layout 跟 paint 都沒有跑。</p>
<p><a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/inside-browser-part3">Inside look, part 3</a> 提到，compositor thread 不用等 JavaScript 或 style 計算，所以 main thread 在忙的時候，<code>transform</code> 跟 <code>opacity</code> 的 CSS 動畫還是會繼續動。<code>left</code>、<code>top</code>、<code>width</code> 的動畫就不一樣了，每個 frame 都要在 main thread 上跑 layout 跟 paint；JavaScript 一直佔著 main thread 的話，frame 就會掉，動畫看起來一頓一頓的。</p>
<h2>九、useEffect</h2>
<p><code>useEffect</code> 通常在瀏覽器 paint 之後才執行。React 文件的用詞是「generally」，例外有三種：</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>click、keydown 這類離散的使用者輸入。</strong> <a href="https://react.dev/blog/2022/03/08/react-18-upgrade-guide">React 18 升級指南</a>寫到，React 18 起，這類更新的 <code>useEffect</code> 會在 paint 之前執行。在 headless Chrome 156 上點一下按鈕之後，React 18.3.1 跟 19.3.1 都在那個 frame paint 之前就跑了 <code>useEffect</code>。effect 本身是在 paint 之前跑沒錯，可是它裡面 setState 再排的 render，在第三節的 tooltip 測試裡 10 次都落到 paint 之後。</li>
<li><strong>其他來源，像 timer 或網路回應。</strong> React 一般會先讓瀏覽器 paint，但沒有保證。同樣在 Chrome 156 上，<code>setTimeout</code> 觸發的更新，React 19.3.1 在 paint 之後才跑 <code>useEffect</code>；React 18.3.1 則是三次都在下一個 frame 之前就跑了。</li>
<li><strong>在 <code>useLayoutEffect</code> 裡 setState。</strong> 照 <a href="https://react.dev/reference/react/useLayoutEffect">react.dev</a> 的說明，這時 React 會立刻把還沒跑的 effect 全部跑完，<code>useEffect</code> 也包括在內。</li>
</ul>
<p>所以 <code>useEffect</code> 在 paint 之前或之後跑都有可能，就算在 paint 之前跑，它裡面 setState 改的畫面也可能趕不上這次 paint。它適合放早一點、晚一點都沒差的事：抓資料、訂閱、掛 event listener。以搜尋框來說，就是向 server 要搜尋結果的那個請求。一定要在 paint 之前做的事放 <code>useLayoutEffect</code>。<a href="https://react.dev/reference/react/useEffect">react.dev</a> 寫到，一定要等 paint 之後才做的事，例如 <code>alert()</code>，要再包一層 <code>setTimeout</code>。假設搜尋框旁邊有一個「清除」按鈕，按下去會清空結果，再跳一個 <code>alert</code> 說已清除。這是 click 觸發的更新，所以 <code>useEffect</code> 可能在 paint 之前就跑。如果在裡面直接呼叫 <code>alert()</code>，舊的清單還留在畫面上，對話框就先跳出來了。而且 <code>alert</code> 會停住 main thread，使用者按下確定之前，清單都不會從畫面上消失：</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">function</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1"> handleClear</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">() {</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  setResults</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">([]);</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  setCleared</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">(</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">true</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">);</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">}</span></span>

<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">  // alert('已清除'); // 可能在清單消失之前就跳出來</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">  const</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5"> id</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49"> =</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1"> setTimeout</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">(() </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=></span><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1"> alert</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">(</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62">'已清除'</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">), </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">0</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">);</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">  return</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> () </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=></span><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1"> clearTimeout</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">(id);</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">}, [cleared]);</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p><code>setTimeout</code> 把 <code>alert</code> 排到下一個 task，瀏覽器通常會先把這個 frame 畫完再執行它。</p>
<h2>「render」這個字的兩個意思</h2>
<p>前端講「render」有兩個意思，混在一起用的話，討論效能時很容易各講各的。</p>

















<table><thead><tr><th>名詞</th><th>意思</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>React 的 render 階段</td><td>執行元件的 function，產生 Virtual DOM。瀏覽器沒有參與。</td></tr><tr><td>瀏覽器的 Render Tree</td><td>DOM 加上 CSSOM 合起來的結果，從 React 在 commit 階段寫好的真實 DOM 建出來。</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>React 的 render 階段產生的是 JavaScript 物件，瀏覽器的 Render Tree 是從真的 DOM 節點建出來的，兩者沒有重疊。同一次更新裡，React 會先做完 render 跟 commit，瀏覽器才用新的 DOM 建 Render Tree。transition 的 render 可能做到一半就暫停，這段期間瀏覽器照樣畫出 frame，畫的是舊的 DOM。</p>
<h2>從開啟頁面到 app 跑起來</h2>
<p>CSS 慢，React 會不會也跟著晚開始呢？React 的 bundle 用 <code>defer</code> 或 <code>type="module"</code> 載入的話會，CSS 晚 1.5 秒到，React 就晚 1.5 秒才開始跑。用 <code>async</code> 載入的話不會，script 下載完就執行，不等 CSS。Vite 7.3.7 <code>vite build</code> 出來的 <code>index.html</code> 用的是 <code>type="module"</code>，這個網站用 Next.js 15.5.12 App Router build 出來的頁面則是 <code>async</code>。</p>
<p>在 headless Chrome 156 上可以這樣驗證：讓 server 故意晚 1.5 秒才回 stylesheet，script 檔則馬上回，然後記下 script 在第幾 ms 開始執行，以及第一個畫面（first contentful paint）在第幾 ms 畫出來。script 早就下載好了，如果它還是拖到 1.5 秒才執行，就代表它在等 CSS。每種頁面各跑三次，<code>defer</code> 跟 <code>type="module"</code> 另外把 script 移到 <code>&#x3C;link></code> 前面，再跑三次：</p>



































<table><thead><tr><th>頁面上的 script</th><th>script 什麼時候執行</th><th><code>DOMContentLoaded</code></th><th>第一個畫面</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>沒有</td><td>—</td><td>6 到 8 ms</td><td>1528 到 1536 ms</td></tr><tr><td><code>defer</code></td><td>1511 到 1522 ms</td><td>跟 script 同時</td><td>1520 到 1532 ms</td></tr><tr><td><code>type="module"</code></td><td>1508 到 1516 ms</td><td>跟 script 同時</td><td>1516 到 1528 ms</td></tr><tr><td><code>async</code></td><td>8 到 11 ms</td><td>6 到 9 ms</td><td>1520 到 1532 ms</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p><code>defer</code> 跟 <code>type="module"</code> 的 script 寫在 <code>&#x3C;link></code> 前面或後面，結果都一樣。照 HTML 規格的 <a href="https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html#the-end">"The end"</a> 這一節，parse 完之後，只要文件裡還有 stylesheet 沒下載完，defer 的 script 就先等，等 stylesheet 都到了才執行。就算 stylesheet 寫在 script 後面，只要 parser 讀到了，defer 的 script 也一樣要等它。<code>async</code> 的 script 不走這段流程，所以不用等。</p>
<p>不過 <code>async</code> 只讓 React 的程式早一點開始跑。script 在 8 到 11 ms 就執行了，可是 stylesheet 還沒到，瀏覽器就不會把畫面畫出來。表格最後一欄是實測結果：用 <code>async</code> 的頁面，第一個畫面也要到 1520 到 1532 ms 才出現，跟 <code>defer</code> 差不多。</p>
<pre><code>瀏覽器收到 HTML
  │
  ├── HTML parser ──► DOM
  │                    │
  │                    ├──► React bundle 執行            ← defer / module：等頁面上所有的 stylesheet
  │                    │                                    async：下載完就跑，不等 CSS
  │                    │       → createRoot(#root).render(&#x3C;App />)
  │                    │       → render + commit        React 寫入 DOM 節點（app 從這裡開始運作）
  │                    ├──► DOMContentLoaded             ← DOM 解析完 + defer/module script 跑完
  │                    │
  └── 下載 CSS ──► CSSOM
                       │
      DOM + CSSOM ─────┴──► Render Tree ──► Layout ──► Paint ──► Composite ──► First Contentful Paint
                            ↑ 要等 CSS 到了才會走到這裡，async 的 React 先 render 完也一樣

  scripts   &#x3C;script>               卡住 parser；等前面的 stylesheet 到了才執行
            &#x3C;script defer>         平行下載；parse 完、所有 stylesheet 都到了才執行
            &#x3C;script async>         平行下載；下載完就執行
            &#x3C;script type="module"> 跟 defer 一樣延後執行，而且有自己的 scope

window.onload      ← 圖片、字型、iframe 都載完；app 通常早就在跑了

──────────────── 之後每一次更新 ────────────────────────────────

任何 setState（event handler、fetch、timer、WebSocket……）
  → 呼叫 setState
      ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │  render 階段      VDOM 比對；transition 才可中斷 │
      │  commit 階段      寫入真實 DOM                   │
      │  useLayoutEffect  讀 layout，卡住 paint          │
      │  Style Recalc     cascade、specificity、換算     │
      │  Render Tree      DOM + computed style           │
      │  Layout / Reflow  幾何：位置、尺寸               │
      │  Paint            每個 layer 的 paint record     │
      │  Composite        layer → GPU → 螢幕             │
      │  useEffect        side effect（點擊觸發的更新    │
      │                   會在 paint 之前跑）            │
      └────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                               │ 任何 setState
                               └──► 回到 render 階段
</code></pre>
<blockquote>
<p><strong>三個 paint 指標。</strong> 上面頁面載入那段路的終點是 <em>FCP</em>（First Contentful Paint），也就是 DOM 裡的文字或圖片第一次畫出來的時間。旁邊還有兩個相關的指標。<a href="https://w3c.github.io/paint-timing/">Paint Timing</a> 定義的 <em>FP</em>（First Paint）是任何像素第一次畫出來的時間，畫了一個非預設的背景色也算。照 <a href="https://web.dev/articles/lcp">web.dev</a> 的說明，<em>LCP</em>（Largest Contentful Paint）是視窗裡最大的那張圖片、那段文字或那支影片畫出來的時間。如果最大的元素是圖片，LCP 就要等那張圖下載完。</p>
</blockquote>
<p>只要 app 還開著，這個迴圈就會一直跑。下面這張時間軸把同一個迴圈攤開，可以對照這九個步驟分別落在哪些 process 跟 thread 上：</p>
<iframe src="/embeds/browser-arch" width="100%" height="880" style="border:none;" title="Browser Architecture: Chrome processes and threads"></iframe>
<h2>參考資料</h2>
<p><strong>React 內部</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><a href="/v2/inside-react-fiberworkloop">Inside React's FiberWorkLoop</a>。我寫的續篇，放大上面「render 階段」跟「commit 階段」這兩項，照編號走過 React reconciler 內部 workloop 的四個階段。</li>
<li><a href="https://react.iamkasong.com">React 技术揭秘</a>，卡颂著。簡體中文，深入講 Fiber、Scheduler、Lanes 跟 Hooks，是從原始碼層級講 React 最常被引用的一本。原始碼在 GitHub 的 <a href="https://github.com/BetaSu/just-react">BetaSu/just-react</a>。</li>
<li><a href="https://7km.top/main/reconciler-workflow">图解React：reconciler 运作流程</a>。另一份簡體中文資料，一個 function 一個 function 講，從 <code>scheduleUpdateOnFiber</code> 分四步走到 <code>commitRoot</code>，附一張呼叫關係圖。可以跟卡颂那本搭著看，流程比較具體。</li>
<li><a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZCuYPiUIONs">A Cartoon Intro to Fiber</a>，Lin Clark 在 React Conf 2017 的演講，用圖解釋 Fiber 為什麼取代了舊的 stack reconciler。</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>瀏覽器 rendering pipeline</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/inside-browser-part1/">Inside look at modern web browser</a>，Mariko Kosaka 寫的四篇系列，講 Chrome 的 process 跟 thread 怎麼分工。</li>
<li><a href="https://web.dev/articles/howbrowserswork">How browsers work</a>，Tali Garsiel 跟 Paul Irish 寫的長文經典，從收到 bytes 一路講到畫出像素。</li>
<li><a href="https://dev.to/arikaturika/how-web-browsers-work-the-render-tree-part-7-with-illustrations-24h3">How web browsers work: the render tree (part 7)</a>，Arika O 在 dev.to 的圖解系列第 7 篇，用圖一步一步講 render tree 怎麼建出來。</li>
<li><a href="https://medium.com/@regondaakhil/the-anatomy-of-browser-rendering-how-web-pages-come-to-life-6fa9e801a3f">The Anatomy of Browser Rendering</a>，Akhil Regonda 寫的，從 parse 到 composite 分六步講，沿路附上優化建議。</li>
<li><a href="https://juejin.cn/post/6952878811046215711">浏览器是如何渲染网页的？</a>，Kerb 把 Uday Hiwarale 的文章翻成簡體中文。講 DOM、CSSOM、render tree，也講會卡住 render 的 CSS 跟會卡住 parser 的 script 怎麼改變整個流程。</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Critical Rendering Path</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://web.dev/articles/critical-rendering-path/render-tree-construction">Render Tree Construction</a>，Ilya Grigorik。DOM 跟 CSSOM 怎麼合起來，哪些節點放進去、哪些拿掉。</li>
<li><a href="https://web.dev/articles/critical-rendering-path/measure-crp">Measure the Critical Rendering Path</a>，Ilya Grigorik。用 Navigation Timing API 跟 Lighthouse 量 CRP 的時間，也說明為什麼只靠 DevTools 不適合量這個。</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Layout 跟 reflow</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://kellegous.com/j/2013/01/26/layout-performance/">On Layout &#x26; Web Performance</a>，Kelly Norton。講 layout thrashing 的經典文章：瀏覽器等到需要才算 layout，所以讀、寫、讀交錯的話，每次都會強制 reflow。</li>
<li><a href="https://web.dev/articles/avoid-large-complex-layouts-and-layout-thrashing">Avoid large, complex layouts and layout thrashing</a>，Jeremy Wagner、Paul Lewis、Barry Pollard。具體做法有三個：先讀再寫、避免強制同步 layout、DOM 不要太大。</li>
<li><a href="https://stackoverflow.com/questions/27637184/what-is-dom-reflow/27637245#27637245">What is DOM reflow?</a>，Stack Overflow 上的問答，簡短說明 reflow 是什麼、哪些動作會觸發。</li>
<li><a href="https://github.com/vasanthk/browser-rendering-optimization/blob/master/README.md">Browser Rendering Optimization</a>，Vasanth Krishnamoorthy 整理 Paul Lewis 跟 Cameron Pittman 在 Udacity 那門課的筆記，主題是怎麼做到 60fps，講 pipeline 每一步、每個 frame 的時間預算，還有每一步各自的優化方法。</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>擴充</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Houdini_APIs">Houdini APIs</a>，MDN。Houdini 讓網頁開發者能介入 CSS 引擎內部的步驟。Paint、Layout、Animation 三種 Worklet 原本設計成各自接進上面 pipeline 的其中一步，不過正式上線的只有 Paint Worklet，而且只有 Chrome 跟 Edge 支援。Houdini 的其他部分，例如 <code>@property</code>，Firefox 跟 Safari 也能用。</li>
<li><a href="https://bitsofco.de/web-workers-vs-service-workers-vs-worklets/">Web Workers vs Service Workers vs Worklets</a>，Ire Aderinokun。簡短比較三者各做什麼；三者裡面，接進 rendering pipeline 的是 Worklet。</li>
